title: Generator Exchange Symmetry in the Proportions of the Great Sphinx of Giza
content: In the Great Sphinx of Giza, the proportions of the lion’s trunk and the height of the human head predict the distance between the elbows. Applying a reciprocal rule to Mark Lehner’s survey gives 18.52 m from the chest and 18.47 m from the haunch against a measured 18.50 m. The rule inverts the ratio of half the chest width to waist width to give the ratio of half the elbow span to head height. With the generator ratio free, only these five landmarks among 12 survey dimensions from two adjacent sections satisfy both identities under the stated rounding model, up to interchange of waist width and head height. The fraction 7/11 fits as closely as any positive real ratio under this interval criterion and has the smallest compatible denominator, followed by 26/41. Within 1,050 template classes, the identities uniquely determine the exchange for the named roles. Comparable fits occurred in 11 of 600,000 fixed-role reference geometries. Given the observed body grid, exact integration gives 0.188% for the specified 22/7 exchange under independent sampling in the central panel and 0.471% with perfectly matched ranks. This coordination supports intentional proportional planning in the preserved Great Sphinx.
